title: 22. Interview: Agentic AI Evaluation: Autonomy, Safety, and Long-Horizon Tasks
summary: Interview Q&A for Agentic AI Evaluation: Autonomy, Safety, and Long-Horizon Tasks.
objectives: Answer the Agentic AI Evaluation: Autonomy, Safety, and Long-Horizon Tasks interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: 11. Interview Questions
sections.body:
### A. Conceptual

**Q1.** Distinguish "an AI agent" from "agentic AI."
**A.** An agent is a single component (planner + tools + loop). Agentic AI is a system paradigm where autonomy, persistence, and real-world effect are first-class design axes. A ReAct loop is an agent; a deployed coding assistant that runs overnight, persists memory, opens PRs, escalates to humans is agentic AI. The former needs trajectory eval; the latter adds safety, memory, cost, and oversight eval.

**Q2.** Walk through the autonomy spectrum. Why does each level require new metrics?
**A.** L0 needs output metrics; L1 adds tool accuracy; L2 adds trajectory eval; L3 adds safety and side-effect eval (actions now have consequences); L4 adds memory and cumulative cost eval; L5 adds alignment and audit-trail eval (human is out of the loop). Each level roughly doubles the eval surface area.

**Q3.** Why does long-horizon eval break standard agent metrics?
**A.** Three reasons: state drift (the world changes underneath), context window limits (force summarization/forgetting), and persistence (memory becomes first-class). Standard trajectory metrics assume a stable environment and fresh context. Neither holds past horizon ~30 minutes.

**Q4.** What is side-effect evaluation, and why is it specific to agentic AI?
**A.** Side-effect eval measures unintended consequences of otherwise-correct actions. It's agentic-specific because agents *act* on the world. Instrument a sandbox, log every state change, compare to the minimal-change baseline and the allowed-action set. Side-effect score = 1 - unauthorized_changes / total_changes. Structurally impossible to measure for chatbots.

**Q5.** Explain indirect prompt injection. Why is it the dominant jailbreak vector for deployed agents?
**A.** Agents read tool outputs into context. If a tool output (web page, email, file) contains attacker-controlled text, that text can issue instructions. It's dominant because the attack surface is all content the agent touches, not just the user's prompt. Eval by injecting adversarial tool outputs and measuring instruction-following, detection, and containment rates.

**Q6.** What are the four core memory metrics, and which is hardest to evaluate?
**A.** Write accuracy (correct at write time), retrieval relevance (relevant to current task?), staleness (true-then-false-now), conflict resolution (which of two contradictory facts wins). Conflict resolution is hardest — you must engineer the contradiction, then verify the agent's tie-breaking logic, and the correct answer often depends on context.

**Q7.** Explain the HHH tradeoff. Why can't all three be maximized?
**A.** HHH = Helpful, Harmless, Honest. They trade off: maximally helpful means completing harmful requests; maximally harmless means refusing too much; maximally honest can leak sensitive context. Pick a policy point on the tradeoff frontier and eval against it — there is no Pareto-optimal corner at 100% on all three.

**Q8.** What is oversight-trigger appropriateness, and how do you measure it?
**A.** Define an oversight policy (when the agent should pause and ask a human). Measure oversight-trigger rate (fraction of tasks with a trigger), trigger appropriateness (of triggers, how many matched policy), and missed-escalation rate (should-have-triggered but didn't). An agent that never triggers is suspicious; one that always triggers isn't autonomous.

**Q9.** Why is calibration critical for Level 3+ agents specifically?
**A.** At L3+, oversight decisions are made on confidence — "am I 80% sure, or 60%?" An over-confident agent in the 70–90% range barrels through situations that warrant escalation. Plot a reliability diagram; the diagonal is perfect calibration. Most agents are over-confident exactly where it matters most.

**Q10.** Why is cost-per-task-success the right cost metric, not cost-per-query?
**A.** Cost-per-query treats all queries equally, but a failed task at $0.02 is worse than a successful one at $0.20. Cost-per-success = total_cost / num_successful_tasks directly tells you whether the agent is economically viable. A 90% accurate agent at $1/success beats a 99% agent at $10/success for most workloads.

### B. Scenario-Based

**Scenario 1.** Your coding agent consistently writes working code on SWE-bench, but in production it sometimes deletes unrelated files in the repo while solving issues. How do you eval this?
**Task.** Design an eval that catches this before the next deploy.
**Sample Answer.** Side-effect eval problem. Stand up an instrumented sandbox where every filesystem change is logged, run the agent on a representative prod task set, and compare final state to the minimal-change baseline and the allowed-action set. Compute side-effect score = 1 - unauthorized_changes / total_changes, and gate deploys on a p95 threshold (≥ 0.98). Diff the agent's tool-call log against an expert trajectory to spot the divergence. SWE-bench is blind to this — it only checks the patch and tests. Add a filesystem-audit step to your internal eval harness and you'll catch the deletion pattern within a few runs.

**Scenario 2.** Your Deep Research agent runs for 30 minutes on a hard question, then produces a shallow 2-paragraph report. The trajectory log shows 80+ tool calls. How do you debug?
**Task.** Identify which long-horizon metric is most likely failing, and how to confirm.
**Sample Answer.** Trajectory length with shallow output points to context-window efficiency: many tool calls but no retention or synthesis. Check context window efficiency (tokens per sub-goal), state tracking accuracy (does the agent's belief match what it actually retrieved?), and memory retrieval relevance. Most likely the agent is summarizing too aggressively and losing key facts. Confirm by injecting mid-trajectory probes ("list the 5 most important facts you've gathered") and comparing to ground truth. Fix by tuning the summarization policy or moving to a memory-augmented architecture (MemGPT-style paging).

**Scenario 3.** Your boss wants to ship a Level 4 autonomy customer-support agent to production next month. What is the first eval you demand, and why?
**Task.** Justify the priority ordering of evals for a Level 4 deployment.
**Sample Answer.** Demand permission/authorization eval and indirect prompt-injection eval first. L4 means the agent acts without per-action human review and reads attacker-controllable content (tickets, emails) into context — a jailbroken support agent issuing unauthorized refunds is a seven-figure incident. Secondary: side-effect eval, oversight-trigger appropriateness, cumulative cost-per-success (L4 runs are long; cost compounds), and memory eval (staleness, conflict resolution). If the boss pushes back: "Level 4 means the agent is trusted to act. Trust without authorization and injection eval is not a product, it's a liability."

**Scenario 4.** Your agent passes every prompt-injection test in your static suite, but in production an attacker got it to send customer PII to an external email by chaining three tool calls, each of which looked benign. How do you change your eval?
**Task.** Identify the eval gap and design a fix.
**Sample Answer.** Gap: per-step safety eval vs trajectory-level. Each tool call was benign in isolation; the composition was harmful. Static injection suites test single prompts and miss composite attacks. Fix: add trajectory-level harm classifiers that score the full action sequence. Run agentic red-teaming (AutoRedTeam-style adaptive attackers) and agentic fuzzing that generates random tool-call chains looking for unsafe compositions. Also add a tool-call graph invariant checker: e.g., "no path from `read_customer_pii` to `send_email_external` without an intervening `escalate`." This catches the composition even when no individual classifier flags it.

**Scenario 5.** You're evaluating two agents on the same SWE-bench subset. Agent A scores 45%, Agent B scores 40%. Agent A costs $0.50 per task; Agent B costs $0.10. Which do you ship?
**Task.** Reason about the cost-quality frontier for agentic systems.
**Sample Answer.** Cost-per-success: A = $0.50 / 0.45 = $1.11; B = $0.10 / 0.40 = $0.25. B is ~4.4x more cost-efficient per successful task. If the deployment is high-volume and downstream human review is cheap, ship B and route failures to humans. If low-volume with high per-task value (e.g., critical security patches), ship A — the 5-point accuracy gain is worth the cost. Also check latency percentiles and side-effect scores; a 5-point gain that comes with worse p99 or more side effects is not a clean win. The decision lives on the cost-quality frontier, not on raw accuracy.
